sanguine

SANG-gwin -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, SANG. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sanguine is optimistic or positive.

Though ticket sales started slowly, the festival's organizer stayed sanguine, certain that word would spread.

Worked Example

The rookie robotics team places dead last at its first meet. On the bus home, the team captain is already grinning over her notebook: 'Our drivetrain held up and our code ran clean -- by spring we'll be in the top ten.'

The captain is sanguine: her outlook is optimistic and positive even while the present looks bleak. Sanguine describes a settled, hopeful way of looking at the future -- not a burst of joy over good news, but calm confidence that things will turn out well.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

optimistic: Optimistic means expecting things to turn out well -- an optimistic forecast, an optimistic fan. Sanguine is optimism settled into temperament: calm, steady, and hard to shake, so a sanguine person keeps expecting good things even while the news is bad.

upbeat: Upbeat describes the mood of the moment -- cheerful, bright, bouncing through the day. Sanguine sits deeper than mood: it is a settled outlook about how things will end, and a sanguine person may not be smiling at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pessimistic: expecting the worst to happen

gloomy: dark and without hope

Where it sits · how settled the positive outlook is — hopeful → sanguine → assured

hopeful vs. sanguine: Hopeful is the everyday, weaker word -- you can be hopeful about one test result -- while sanguine describes a whole optimistic outlook that stays steady even when the news turns bad.

assured vs. sanguine: Assured is more settled still than sanguine: a sanguine person expects things to work out while granting that they might not, but an assured one treats success as already a fact, with no doubt left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sangu-

Root — sangu-: blood (from Latin sanguis, sanguinem, 'blood')

Suffix — -ine

Suffix — -ine: of or like (Latin -ineus)

Put it together

Put it together: Sanguine is literally 'of blood': sangu- (from Latin sanguis, 'blood') + -ine ('of or like'). Medieval doctors taught that a person with plenty of blood among their four bodily humors would be ruddy, cheerful, and confident -- so 'blood-like' came to mean hopeful and optimistic, and that temperament sense is the one English kept.

Use the root in a new word: sanguinary

Use the root in a new word: sanguinary: The historian called it the most sanguinary battle of the entire war.

Word Building

Word Choice

Sanguine describes a lasting outlook, not a momentary thrill: sanguine about the future, sanguine about the team's chances. Keep it apart from elated, its cluster neighbor, which names a short spike of joy set off by one piece of good news -- a sanguine person may not even be smiling; they simply expect things to work out.
